author: Toni Viola
title: The Cause Of All Fear
text:
08:15 Wednesday 25 October 2017
Molino Bar & Cucina, Rome
Meroni ran. Ignoring the pain in his ribs, he sprinted up the road leading away from Piazza dell’Esquilino, weaving in and out of the slow-moving traffic, and dodging the pedestrians in Piazza di Santa Maggiore; he did not stop, or look back, until he entered Molino on Via Merulana. It was a popular bakery and restaurant, full of early morning customers. Plenty of cover. He could blend in. Meroni removed his helmet, took out his phone and hit speed dial for Teresa Conti. 
Engaged tone. 
Nodding at a member of staff, Meroni walked over to the street-facing counter. A perfect vantage point to watch and wait. He caught his reflection in the mirror to his right; apart from a tear at the knee of his jeans, his clothing had survived the fall. He dusted the road grit from the sleeve of his leather jacket and turned to grab a stool. The sudden movement caused the pain to shoot through his body. The bicycle pedal had caught him in the ribs as he tumbled into the hapless cyclist. He probed his chest and abdomen. Bruises, nothing broken.
Meroni sat down. His left leg shook with nervous impatience as he scanned the scene outside: cars, buses, mopeds, cyclists, people. Thousands of individual orbits revolving in synch around Rome, proof eternal of Newton’s first law of motion. 
Meroni dialled again.
Pick up, Teresa ...
‘Pronto.’
‘Teresa?’
‘Missing me already, Meroni?’
‘Where are you?’
‘Why are you whispering?’
‘Are you in a taxi, Teresa?’
‘Yes, but I can barely hear you.’
Meroni checked the other customers. Nobody was listening to his conversation. He spoke a little louder. ‘Get the driver to come to Molino, on Via Merulana.’ 
A girl came over to serve him. Meroni held up two fingers and jerked his thumb over his shoulder – a double shot of espresso to go. 
‘Why do I need to come to Via Merulana?’ 
‘I’ll tell you when you get here. Make sure the driver avoids Piazza dell’Esquilino because there’s been an accident.’
‘Are you okay?’
‘Yes, I’m fine. I take it you’re in the back seat?’
‘Of course.’
‘When you get to Via Merulana, make yourself invisible.’
‘What are you talking about, Luca?’
‘There are quite a few people in here. They’ll recognise you and I don’t want to draw any unnecessary attention. What make of taxi are you in?’
‘I don’t know.’
‘Could you ask the driver, Teresa?’
‘Wait … Driver, what car are we in?’ There was a muffled response. ‘It’s an Opel.’
‘Which model?’ 
‘Driver … What model?’ Again, the sound of somebody speaking in the background. ‘It’s a Meriva.’
‘What colour is the taxi?’
‘Are you serious?’
‘What colour is the taxi, Teresa?’
‘It’s a white taxi … you know what colour the taxi is. All the proper taxis in Rome are white. What’s going on?’
‘I’ll see you soon.’ Meroni ended the call and kept watch outside. His leg was still shaking. He couldn’t help but smile at Teresa’s insistence that she was in a “proper” taxi. All cabs with an official licence in Rome were white. He should have known she wouldn’t ride with a budget firm.
Meroni dialled Russo’s number.
‘Pronto.’
‘Russo, have a look outside your apartment …’
‘Morning, Meroni. How are you? I’m fine, thanks. How are you? Oh, I’m fine too, thank you for asking …’
‘No time, Roberta. What do you see from your window?’
He had called her by her first name. It was a verbal signal, a prompt.
‘Okay, there is a thick-set male stood on the opposite pavement. Olive-skinned, bald, tattoos on his neck, leather jacket, smoking … a southerner. Is this a test? I like tests.’
‘Stop taking the piss and keep watching …’
Meroni could hear Russo humming. Sometimes she could be infuriating.
‘He just nodded to somebody else up the street. I can’t see who. Wait … there’s an Alfa Romeo – black on Napoli plates. Nice car.’
The Alfa Romeo was getting around fast. He had last seen it less than ten minutes ago, and yet it had negotiated the rush-hour traffic and made it to her apartment.
‘Listen, Russo. The Alfa followed me, they’ll wait to see if I turn up at yours. Don’t go outside until they’ve gone and keep an eye out for the car. I’m going home.’      
‘What about the murders?’
‘I need time to think.’
‘And Gambarella will buy that?’
‘He’ll have to. I haven’t returned to the Questura – still officially on sick leave, remember. I’ll call you later.’
‘I might have plans.’
‘Have fun.’
‘Girls usually do.’
Meroni hung up and called Gambarella.
‘Pronto.’
‘Gamba, any more news about the Colosseum?’
‘I was hoping you might have something for me,’ said Gambarella.
Meroni remained silent.
‘That tells me everything I need to know. I spoke with the senior officer in Siena. There’s nothing more from their case other than what we already know. Body found, old-fashioned clothing, papers, no DNA, or fingerprint hit. The media are clamouring for more information, Meroni. I’ve already fielded three calls from la cagna this morning.’
It was the tabloid press who had first called Teresa, the 'Bitch'. Her reputation was one of a hard-nosed and formidable journalist. She intimidated most men; hence, the derogatory nickname. Teresa didn’t suffer fools, so why had she been so desperate to get hold of Gambarella this morning? She had other sources within the Questura.
A white Opel Meriva taxi stopped on the opposite side of the road.
‘Boss, could you get one of your uniform boys to pick up my Vespa from the junction of Via Cavour and Piazza dell’Esquilino. Slight accident involving a bus … Oh, and you might receive a report of a shooting incident in the street market near to my apartment.’
‘What the …’
Meroni hung up. Immediately, his phone rang. The inspector calling him back.
Meroni declined the call.
The girl returned with his coffee. He took the paper cup and handed her five euros. ‘Keep the change.’
She smiled and pocketed the note.
Meroni exited and jogged across the road to the waiting taxi. He got in the front passenger seat. ‘Stazione Termini please, driver.’
‘Meroni, what is this awful mess you’ve gotten into?’ asked Teresa. ‘Why are you going to the train station, and please explain why I’m having to lie down on the back seat of a taxi?’
Meroni turned and looked down at her. ‘Multiple questions? Bad interview technique, Signora Giornalista.’ 
Teresa pulled a face. Meroni put his fingers to her lips. He cast his eyes towards the taxi driver. Now was not the time to talk. 
The taxi moved off. Meroni looked out the back window. There was no vehicle following behind. The clumsy efforts of the Alfa Romeo were a deliberate attempt to draw him in. The bullet fired at him was wide of the mark. It wasn’t as if the Vespa was a fast-moving target. The shooter had aimed low, intending to miss him. And now, the Alfa Romeo was in Via Sistina outside Russo’s apartment. Something was going down.
There was only one place to go. A safe space. Out of harm’s way. He needed to remove himself from the equation. Meroni’s mood darkened. He couldn’t grasp at answers when he didn’t know the questions. He would anger Gambarella by going, but he was so tired. His mind was all over the place; he needed more time to reset. 
He was going home. To Cassino.
Teresa had lapsed into silence. Upon waking this morning, he had found her in the kitchen. Usually, she sneaked out early from the apartment, headed home, and then to work, leaving him asleep in bed. This morning, she had hung around. Apart from asking whether Inspector Gambarella had finally persuaded him to return to the Questura and assigned him to the murder at the Colosseum, she had said little else. Not like her at all.
The taxi pulled into the rank outside the station. Meroni gestured for Teresa to sit up. 
She moved behind him, leant forward, and whispered into his ear. ‘Please tell me what’s going on.’
That was more like Teresa. Digging for a story.
The taxi driver grinned. 
Meroni sang, ‘Woman is flighty, like a feather in the wind …’
It was a joke. She had been at the opera yesterday evening and by her own admission she was a fickle woman. But when Meroni sang the duke’s canzone, Teresa recoiled.
Meroni exited the taxi and opened a rear door. Teresa shuffled across the back seat. He thrust his crash helmet at her and slammed the door shut. 
‘Via Margutta.’ Meroni handed the driver twenty euros through the open window. 
Teresa slumped forward and rested her forehead on the helmet. 
Meroni stared after the taxi as it drove away. He didn’t like this version of Teresa Conti.
But it wasn’t just her. Everything was off.
Meroni turned and entered the station, allowing himself to be swallowed up by the great swarm of humanity.
He downed his espresso.
He needed to escape.
He studied the departures board. Thirty minutes until the next train to Cassino – plenty of time for more coffee.
